questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: What is the capital city of Australia?
questions.explain: Canberra, in the Australian Capital Territory, is the nation's capital. Parliament House, the High Court of Australia and several other national institutions are located there, roughly midway between Sydney and Melbourne.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: How many states and mainland territories make up Australia?
options: Six states and two mainland territories
questions.explain: Australia, officially the Commonwealth of Australia, is a federation formed by six states plus two territories on the mainland. Canberra serves as the national capital, and every state and mainland territory has a capital city of its own.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: When is Australia Day celebrated?
questions.explain: Australia Day falls on 26 January every year, and all states and territories observe it as a public holiday. The date recalls the landing of the First Fleet, which sailed from Great Britain and arrived in 1788.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: On which date is Anzac Day commemorated?
questions.explain: Anzac Day is held on 25 April. On that date in 1915, during World War I, Australian and New Zealand soldiers went ashore at Gallipoli in Türkiye. It is a solemn occasion to honour everyone who served and died in wars.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: What is Australia's national flower?
questions.explain: The golden wattle is the national flower. It is a small tree found mostly in Australia's south-east, with bright green foliage and masses of golden yellow blossoms in spring. Every state and territory has chosen a floral emblem too.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: Who were the first inhabitants of Australia?
options: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
questions.explain: The first people to live in Australia were the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. Their cultures and traditions are the world's oldest continuous cultures, and their strong bond with the land is expressed through stories, art and dance.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 1: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: Where do Torres Strait Islander people come from?
options: Islands lying between Queensland's northern tip and Papua New Guinea
The western coast of Western Australia
questions.explain: Torres Strait Islander people come from the islands that lie between Papua New Guinea and the northern tip of Queensland. Aboriginal people historically come from mainland Australia and Tasmania. Together they are Australia's first peoples.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 1: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: According to the archaeological record, when did Aboriginal peoples arrive in Australia?
questions.explain: Archaeological evidence shows that Aboriginal peoples reached Australia somewhere between 40,000 and 65,000 years ago. Aboriginal peoples themselves hold that they are at the heart of this land's creation stories, which start at the beginning of time.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 1: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: How many convict ships made up the First Fleet that arrived from Great Britain in 1788?
questions.explain: European settlement started on 26 January 1788, when the First Fleet of 11 convict ships reached Australia from Great Britain. Because British jails were overcrowded, the government sent convicts to the newly founded colony of New South Wales.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 1: Early days of European settlement

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: Who served as the first Governor of New South Wales when it was a colony?
questions.explain: Captain Arthur Phillip was the first Governor of New South Wales as a colony. The settlement survived and expanded as more convicts and free settlers came, and other colonies were later founded in different parts of Australia.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 1: Early days of European settlement

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: In which year did a gold rush start in the colonies of Victoria and New South Wales?
questions.explain: A gold rush began in 1851 when gold was discovered in New South Wales and Victoria. People came from all around the world to seek their fortune, and within ten years Australia's population had more than doubled.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 1: Early days of European settlement

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: During the gold rush, which group became the first large wave of migrants from outside Europe?
questions.explain: Chinese people who arrived in the colonies during the gold rush of the 1850s were the first large group of migrants to Australia who did not come from Europe. They added to the growing diversity of the colonies.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 1: Early days of European settlement

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: After which event were Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples included in official estimates of Australia's population?
options: The end of World War II
questions.explain: In 1901 Australia had about four million people, but this count left out Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. They were only counted in official estimates of the population after the 1967 Referendum.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: What brought a wave of non-British migration to Australia after World War II?
options: The opening of the Sydney Harbour Bridge
Millions of Europeans were forced out of their homelands
questions.explain: After World War II, millions of Europeans were forced out of their homelands. Many of them came to Australia to start a new life, bringing a wave of migration from countries other than Britain.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: What is Australia's national language?
questions.explain: English is the national language and part of Australia's national identity. Speaking English helps people get the most out of life and work in Australia, and Australian values expect migrants to learn and use it.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: How many distinct Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages does the guide say are valued in Australia?
questions.explain: English is the national language, but other languages are valued in Australia too. They include over 100 different languages of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, whose cultures are the world's oldest continuous cultures.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: Which colony did the British establish first in Australia?
questions.explain: New South Wales was the first colony the British founded. Its capital, Sydney, is now the country's largest city, and both the Sydney Harbour Bridge and the Opera House are national icons.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: Which is the smallest of the mainland states?
questions.explain: Victoria is the smallest state on the mainland, and Melbourne is its capital. Wealth from the 1850s gold rush paid for many of Victoria's fine buildings, and its icons include the Melbourne Cricket Ground and the 12 Apostles.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: Which is the largest state in Australia?
questions.explain: Western Australia is the largest state, with Perth as its capital. Most of the eastern part of the state is desert, while the south-west is rich farming and wine country. Many large mining projects operate there.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: The Great Barrier Reef runs along the coast of which state?
questions.explain: The world-famous Great Barrier Reef lies off Queensland's eastern coast. Queensland is the second largest state and its capital is Brisbane. It has tropical rainforests, mild coastal areas and an inland that is often dry.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: What separates Tasmania from the Australian mainland?
questions.explain: Tasmania, the smallest state, is an island divided from the mainland by Bass Strait. Hobart is its capital, much of the island is untouched wilderness, and its well-known sights include Port Arthur, Cradle Mountain and the Bay of Fires.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: Uluru, Kata Tjuta and Kings Canyon are icons of which part of Australia?
questions.explain: Uluru, Kata Tjuta and Kings Canyon are icons of the Northern Territory. Its north is tropical and its south is dry red desert, and its capital city is Darwin.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: Who performs a Welcome to Country?
options: A local custodian who is an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander person
questions.explain: A Welcome to Country is given by a local custodian who is an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander person, welcoming visitors onto their traditional land. It may involve songs, dances, smoking ceremonies or speeches and usually begins an event.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 1: Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: As part of the Australia Day celebrations, who names the Australian of the Year Award winners in Canberra?
questions.explain: As part of Australia Day, it is the Prime Minister who names, in Canberra, the winners of the Australian of the Year Awards. Events are also held across the country on the day, including special citizenship ceremonies.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: Anzac Day takes its name from which military force?
options: The Australian Navy and Air Corps
The Australian and New Zealand Army Corps
questions.explain: Anzac Day takes its name from the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps, the force that landed at Gallipoli in Türkiye in World War I. On the day, Australians honour everyone who served, and those who died, in wars, conflicts and peacekeeping operations.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: What do the seven points of the Commonwealth Star on the Australian National Flag represent?
options: The seven days of the week
The six states and the territories
questions.explain: The Commonwealth Star, beneath the Union Jack on the Australian National Flag, has seven points. Six points represent the six states and one point represents the territories. The Southern Cross appears on the right of the flag.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: On the Australian Aboriginal Flag, what does the yellow circle represent?
questions.explain: The Australian Aboriginal Flag has three colours: black, red and yellow. Its black upper half stands for the Aboriginal peoples of Australia, its red lower half for the earth and its ceremonial significance, and its yellow circle for the sun.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: Which two native animals support the shield on the Commonwealth Coat of Arms?
questions.explain: On the Commonwealth Coat of Arms, a kangaroo and an emu, both native animals, support the shield, which represents the six states and federation. A gold Commonwealth Star sits above, against a background of golden wattle.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: What is Australia's national gemstone?
questions.explain: The national gemstone is the opal. An Aboriginal legend tells that the opal's colours were made when a rainbow touched the earth, and the stone is known for its shifting flashes of colour.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 1: Australia and its people
questions.q: What is the title of Australia's national anthem?
questions.explain: 'Advance Australia Fair' is the national anthem. It is sung at events of national importance, such as citizenship ceremonies and major sporting events. Everyone joins in singing it at a citizenship ceremony.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: For Australian citizens aged 18 or over, enrolling and voting in federal elections is…
questions.explain: Australian citizens aged 18 or over must enrol and vote in federal elections, in elections for their state or territory, and in referendums. Voting gives citizens a say in how Australia is governed, although voting in some local government elections may not be compulsory.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Responsibilities and privileges of Australian citizenship

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: What is Australia's system of government?
questions.explain: Australia is governed as a parliamentary democracy. The government's power comes from the Australian people, since citizens elect people to represent them in parliament. Those elected representatives make the laws.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: In Australia's parliamentary democracy, how do representatives answer to the people for their decisions?
options: They do not answer to anyone
questions.explain: Members of parliament are accountable to the people, through elections, for their decisions. Voters who are unhappy with their representatives can choose someone else at the next election.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: How do Australians believe change in society or the law should come about?
options: Through discussion, peaceful persuasion and democratic processes
questions.explain: Australians value living in a peaceful country whose system of government is stable. They believe change should come through discussion, peaceful persuasion and democratic processes, and they reject violence as a means of changing someone's mind or changing the law.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: How are all Australians expected to treat each other, whatever their race, gender, age, religion or background?
options: According to their country of origin
With suspicion until trust is earned
questions.explain: Australia's democratic system rests on every individual having rights and equality under the law. Australians are expected to treat one another with dignity and respect, whatever their race, origin, gender, sexual orientation, age, disability, religion or wealth.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Respect for all individuals regardless of background

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Under freedom of speech, can people in Australia criticise the government?
options: No, it is against the law
Yes, as long as they obey Australian laws
questions.explain: Freedom of speech means people may speak and write their opinions. For example, they can criticise the government, protest peacefully against its decisions and campaign for laws to change, as long as they still obey Australian laws.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Freedom of expression in Australia includes expressing views through which means?
questions.explain: Freedom of expression means people may share their views, for example through film, art, music and literature. People may also meet in public or in private to discuss social or political matters, provided they always obey the law.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Freedom of speech and freedom of expression

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: When people gather to protest against a government action, what must the gathering be like?
options: Peaceful, without injuring anyone or damaging property
Limited to members of one political party
questions.explain: Australians may join with others to protest against an organisation or a government action. Because the law must always be obeyed, these gatherings have to be peaceful and must not hurt anyone or damage property.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: How does the guide describe Australia's religious heritage?
questions.explain: Australia's heritage is Judaeo-Christian and many Australians identify as Christians, but people of every major religion live in Australia. The government and the law treat every citizen equally, whatever they believe.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Which of these is a public holiday in Australia on a Christian day?
questions.explain: Because of its Judaeo-Christian heritage, Australia observes public holidays on Christian days such as Christmas Day, Good Friday and Easter Sunday. People of every faith, and of no faith, are free to practise their own beliefs.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: The government in Australia is secular. What does this mean?
options: It operates separately from churches and other religious entities
It is run by church leaders
questions.explain: Australia's government is secular: it works separately from churches and other religious bodies. The country has no official national religion, and the government treats every citizen equally, whatever their religion or beliefs.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Is this statement TRUE or FALSE? People in Australia are required to follow a religion.
questions.explain: The statement is false. In Australia people may follow whichever religion they choose, or no religion at all. Either way, religious or not, everyone must obey the laws of Australia.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: What does a 'fair go' mean in Australia?
options: What people achieve should come from their talents, work and effort, not their wealth or background
Only citizens may own a business
questions.explain: Australians value equal opportunity, often called a 'fair go'. What a person achieves in life should depend on their talent, work and effort, not on their wealth or background, so Australian society has no formal class distinctions.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Equality of opportunity and a 'fair go'

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Australian law protects people from being treated differently because of which characteristics?
questions.explain: Several Australian laws make sure nobody is treated differently from other people on the grounds of race, gender, age or disability. Equal treatment under the law is one of Australia's core democratic principles.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Serving in the Australian Defence Force is voluntary. What related responsibility do Australian citizens have?
options: To serve in the army for two years
To pay a defence fee instead
To defend Australia should the need arise
questions.explain: Even though serving in the Australian Defence Force is voluntary, citizens have a responsibility to defend Australia if the need arises. It is essential that citizens are willing to come together to protect the nation and its way of life.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Defend Australia should the need arise

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Which Australian citizens may be called for jury service?
options: Citizens who are on the electoral roll
questions.explain: Serving on a jury when asked is a responsibility of Australian citizens aged 18 or over, and citizens on the electoral roll may be called. A jury of ordinary men and women hears the evidence and decides whether a person is guilty or not guilty.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Serve on a jury if called to do so

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: What is a referendum?
options: A vote to choose a new Prime Minister
A vote to change the Australian Constitution
A survey run by a newspaper
questions.explain: A referendum is a vote on whether to change the Australian Constitution. Voting in one is a responsibility of citizens aged 18 or over, just as voting in federal, state and territory elections is.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Voting in federal and state or territory elections, and in a referendum

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Is voting compulsory in every Australian election?
options: It is compulsory in federal, state and territory elections, but may not be in some local government elections
Only for people born in Australia
questions.explain: Voting is compulsory in federal elections and in state and territory elections. In some states, however, voting in local government elections may be optional. Voting gives citizens a say in how Australia is governed.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Voting in federal and state or territory elections, and in a referendum

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Which is a privilege of Australian citizenship relating to children born overseas?
options: Their automatic exemption from all taxes
Their right to vote from age 12
Applying for them to become Australian citizens by descent
questions.explain: Australian citizens may apply for Australian citizenship by descent for a child of theirs born overseas. This is one of the privileges of citizenship, along with voting, standing for election and holding an Australian passport.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Apply for children born overseas to become Australian citizens by descent

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Which is an example of working in the Australian Public Service, a privilege of citizenship?
options: Working for the Australian Taxation Office
questions.explain: One privilege of Australian citizenship is being able to apply for Australian Public Service jobs, working for the Australian Government at agencies such as the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) or Services Australia.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Apply for work in the Australian Public Service and the Australian Defence Force

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Which three services make up the Australian Defence Force?
options: The Army, Navy and Air Force
The Navy, Customs and Border Force
The Air Force, Fire Brigade and Ambulance
questions.explain: Australian citizens may apply to work in the Australian Defence Force, which consists of the Army, the Navy and the Air Force. Serving in the Defence Force is voluntary.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Apply for work in the Australian Public Service and the Australian Defence Force

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Which Australian citizens CANNOT seek election to parliament?
questions.explain: Australian citizens aged 18 or over who do not hold dual citizenship may stand for election to a federal, state or territory parliament. Serving in an Australian parliament is both an honour and a serious responsibility.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: As an Australian citizen travelling abroad, what do you need to come back to Australia?
options: No visa: you are free to return
questions.explain: Australian citizens may live in Australia freely and have the privilege of applying for an Australian passport. After travelling abroad, they can come back to Australia without needing a visa.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Apply for an Australian passport and re-enter Australia freely

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: When abroad, where can an Australian citizen seek help from Australian government officials in an emergency?
options: An Australian embassy, high commission or consulate
questions.explain: In many countries there is an Australian embassy, high commission or consulate. Australian officials there can help citizens during emergencies such as civil unrest or natural disasters, issue emergency passports and give support after an accident, serious illness or death.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Ask for consular assistance from an Australian official while overseas

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: When an Australian citizen is in another country, whose laws must they obey?
questions.explain: Australian citizens can seek consular help from Australian officials while overseas, but when in another country they must obey the laws of that country. Consular assistance does not place a person above local law.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Ask for consular assistance from an Australian official while overseas

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Which agency collects tax paid on money earned from a job, a business or investments?
questions.explain: Paying tax is a legal requirement and an important way of contributing to the Australian community. Tax is paid on income from employment, a business or investments, and the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) collects it.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Which of these services are paid for through taxes in Australia?
options: Government healthcare and education, defence, roads and social security
questions.explain: Taxes make possible many of the benefits Australians enjoy. They fund government healthcare and education, defence, social security, and roads and railways. Local councils and state and territory governments also raise taxes to pay for services.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Which of these is an example of actively participating in Australian society?
options: Volunteering to do social and community work
questions.explain: Australia encourages all citizens to participate actively in society. Examples include joining neighbourhood and community organisations, volunteering for social and community work, joining an arts or cultural group and taking part in political life.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Is tax in Australia paid only on wages from a job?
options: No, many goods and services are taxed as well
questions.explain: Tax is paid on income from employment, a business or investments, and many goods and services are taxed as well. The ATO helps people understand their tax rights and obligations and makes sure they pay the right amount.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 2: Democratic beliefs, rights and liberties
questions.q: Why do our representatives in government make laws?
options: To benefit only the governing party
To keep society orderly, free and safe and to protect our rights
To limit who can live in each state
questions.explain: Our representatives in government make laws to keep society orderly, free and safe and to protect people's rights. Every Australian citizen, and everyone else in Australia, must obey Australian laws.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 2: Obey the laws of Australia

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: On what date did the colonies unite as the Commonwealth of Australia?
questions.explain: The Australian Constitution took effect on 1 January 1901, and the six colonies joined to form a single independent nation called the Commonwealth of Australia. The national parliament, government and High Court were set up at that time.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: How many senators does each state elect?
questions.explain: Every state has equal representation in the Senate, regardless of its size or population. Each state elects 12 senators, while the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory elect two each, for a total of 76 senators.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Who signs a Bill to make it law (Royal Assent)?
questions.explain: A proposed law, called a Bill, must be agreed by a majority in both Houses of Parliament. It then goes to the Governor-General, whose signature, known as Royal Assent, turns the Bill into law.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Which level of government is mainly responsible for hospitals and schools?
questions.explain: State and territory governments mainly look after schools, hospitals and health services, roads and railways, forestry, police, ambulance services and public transport. Other services are the job of the Australian Government or local councils.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 3: What do the three levels of government do?

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Which agency conducts federal elections and referendums and maintains the Commonwealth electoral roll?
options: The Department of the Prime Minister
questions.explain: The Australian Electoral Commission (AEC) is an agency of the Commonwealth that conducts federal elections and referendums and maintains the electoral roll. It is independent, so neither political parties nor people in government can influence its decisions.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 3: How do I have my say?

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Australian elections use a secret ballot. What does this mean?
options: Nobody is entitled to know how you voted unless you decide to tell them
Votes are counted in secret by the government
Only some people are told about the election
Candidates are kept secret until election day
questions.explain: Because Australia votes by secret ballot, voters can choose any candidate freely and safely. Nobody is entitled to know how you voted, unless you decide to tell them yourself.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 3: How do I have my say?

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Before 1901, how was Australia made up?
options: Two large colonies, east and west
questions.explain: Between British settlement and 1901, Australia consisted of six separate British colonies that governed themselves, each with its own constitution and its own laws on defence, immigration, postage, trade and transport. This caused difficulties between them.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Which court did the Australian Constitution establish, with the final power to apply and interpret Australia's laws?
options: The Supreme Court of New South Wales
questions.explain: The Australian Constitution created the Parliament of the Commonwealth, with two houses: the House of Representatives and the Senate. It also created the High Court of Australia, which holds the final power to apply and interpret Australia's laws.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: What is needed in a referendum for the Australian Constitution to be changed?
options: The agreement of the Prime Minister alone
A two-thirds vote in the Senate only
A majority of voters in New South Wales
A 'double majority': most voters nationally and most voters in a majority of the states
questions.explain: A referendum needs a 'double majority'. Most voters across the whole country must support the change, and most voters in a majority of the states must support it as well.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Why does the Australian Constitution divide the power of government into legislative, executive and judicial powers?
options: To stop one person or group from holding all the power
To give the King more control
To allow the states to ignore federal law
questions.explain: The Constitution divides government power between the legislative (Parliament), the executive (such as the Prime Minister and Cabinet) and the judicial (judges). This separation prevents any one person or group from holding all the power.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 3: How is the power of government controlled?

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: On whose advice does the King of Australia appoint the Governor-General?
options: The Premier of New South Wales
questions.explain: The Governor-General is appointed by the King of Australia to represent him in Australia, on the advice of the Australian Prime Minister. The Governor-General stays independent of every political party and must remain neutral.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 3: Who is Australia's Head of State?

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Who represents the King in each Australian state?
questions.explain: Each of the six states has a Governor who represents the King, much as the Governor-General does for the nation as a whole. The King takes no part in the everyday running of government.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 3: Who is Australia's Head of State?

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Which of these is part of the Governor-General's role?
options: Being Commander-in-Chief of the ADF (Australian Defence Force)
questions.explain: The Governor-General must remain neutral and does not belong to the government. The role includes signing Bills into law, ceremonial duties, approving the appointment of ministers and federal judges, triggering a federal election and serving as Commander-in-Chief of the ADF.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 3: The role of the Governor-General

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: What is the title of the leader of a state government?
questions.explain: A state government is led by the Premier. A territory government is led by the Chief Minister, and a local government is led by a Mayor or Shire President.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 3: Who are some of Australia's leaders?

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Which is another name for the Senate?
questions.explain: The Senate is also known as the Upper House, the States' House or the House of Review. The House of Representatives, by contrast, is known as the People's House, or simply the Lower House.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: What is a key difference between Australian states and self-governing territories?
options: The Australian Government can change or overturn territory laws whenever it chooses
Territories are ruled by the King directly
questions.explain: The Constitution recognises rights for the states but not for the territories. States make laws in their own right, whereas the Australian Government can change or overturn laws made by self-governing territories whenever it chooses.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Which level of government is responsible for immigration and citizenship?
questions.explain: The Australian Government is responsible for matters including taxation, immigration and citizenship, defence, foreign affairs, social security, postal services, trade, and airports and air safety. States and local councils deal with other services.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 3: What do the three levels of government do?

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: After a federal election, who generally forms the Australian Government?
options: The party or coalition with the majority of members in the House of Representatives
The party with the most senators
The party chosen by the Governor-General personally
The party with the oldest leader
questions.explain: After a federal election, the government is usually formed by whichever party or coalition holds most of the seats in the House of Representatives. The leader of that party becomes Prime Minister.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 3: How is the Australian Government formed?

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Who forms the Opposition after a federal election?
options: The party or coalition holding the second highest number of seats in the House of Representatives
Members chosen by the High Court
questions.explain: The Opposition is the party or coalition that wins the second highest number of seats in the House of Representatives. Its leader is known as the Leader of the Opposition, and it closely examines the government's work.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 3: How is the Australian Government formed?

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: When a member of parliament proposes a new law or a change to an existing one, what is the proposal called?
questions.explain: A Bill is a proposal for a new law or for a change to a current law. Both Houses of Parliament consider, debate and vote on it, and if each agrees by a majority, it goes to the Governor-General for Royal Assent.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: The government appoints judges and magistrates. Can it remove them because it disagrees with their decisions?
options: Only if the Prime Minister agrees
questions.explain: Judges and magistrates are the top authority in a courtroom. They are independent, and nobody can instruct them on what to decide. Although the government appoints them, it cannot dismiss them for making decisions it does not like.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: In Australia's court system, how is a person treated unless and until a court finds them guilty?
questions.explain: Australian courts treat people as innocent until a court has found them guilty. Everyone also has the right to a lawyer to represent them in court.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: In a criminal trial, who decides the penalty once a jury has found a person guilty?
questions.explain: A jury is a group of ordinary citizens chosen at random from the population. The judge explains the relevant law to the jurors, the jury decides whether the person is innocent or guilty, and in a criminal trial the judge then sets the penalty.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Besides investigating crimes against federal laws, the Australian Federal Police is responsible for general police work in which place?
questions.explain: The Australian Federal Police (AFP) investigates crimes against federal laws, such as drug trafficking and crimes against national security or the environment. It also does ordinary policing in the Australian Capital Territory.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: In Australia, is it a crime simply to offer a bribe to a police officer?
options: No, only accepting a bribe is a crime
Only if the amount is large
Yes, even offering a bribe is a crime
questions.explain: Bribing the police is a serious crime in Australia, and even offering a police officer a bribe is a crime. The police are independent of government and have a good relationship with the community.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Can you still be charged for breaking an Australian law you were unaware of?
options: Yes, not knowing the law is no excuse
Only if you are a citizen
questions.explain: It is important to be familiar with the laws of Australia. If you break a law you did not know about, you could still be charged, because not knowing the law is no excuse.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Which of these can be a form of domestic and family violence?
options: Cutting a family member off from their friends and family
questions.explain: Domestic and family violence covers behaviour or threats meant to control a partner by making them afraid or putting their safety at risk. Examples include hitting, cutting a family member off from their friends and family, or making threats against pets or children. It is against the law.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Who must wear a seatbelt when travelling in a car in Australia?
questions.explain: Everyone in a car in Australia must wear a seatbelt, and babies and young children must travel in an approved child car seat. State and territory governments set the road rules, and breaking them can lead to fines or prison.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: Is it legal in Australia to drive while using a hand-held mobile device?
options: No, it is against the law
questions.explain: Australia's traffic laws are very strict. Using a hand-held mobile device while driving is illegal, and so is driving after taking drugs or with a blood alcohol level above the limit.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 3: Government and the law in Australia
questions.q: What do you need in order to drive a car in Australia?
options: A local driver's licence and a registered car
Only a foreign licence held for ten years
questions.explain: To drive in Australia you need a driver's licence issued locally, and the vehicle must be registered. State and territory governments control the road and traffic rules, and people who break them can be fined or sent to prison.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Can a religious law override Australian law?
options: No, Australian law prevails over a religious practice
questions.explain: There is no official national religion in Australia, and people may follow any religion or none. Australian laws must be obeyed at all times: if an Australian law and a religious practice conflict, the Australian law takes priority.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Do women and men have equal rights in Australia?
questions.explain: Yes. In Australia, women and men have equal rights. Both can access education and jobs on equal terms, vote and stand for parliament, join the police and the Australian Defence Force, and are treated equally in the courts.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Equality of all people under the law

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Is it acceptable to promote violence against a group because of its religion?
questions.explain: Promoting violence against another person or group is never acceptable, for example on the grounds of their culture, ethnicity, religion or background. It goes against Australian values and against the law, whatever the setting.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Under the Rule of Law, who must obey Australian laws?
questions.explain: Under the Rule of Law, every Australian is equal before the law, and nobody, whether a person or a group, stands above it. Australian laws apply to everyone in Australia, whatever their background or culture.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Commitment to the Rule of Law

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Can a person be forced to join or stay in an organisation?
options: No, joining or leaving is voluntary
questions.explain: People in Australia may join or leave any lawful group of their own free will, such as a political party, a trade union, or a religious, cultural or social group. Nobody can be forced to join an organisation or made to leave one.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Under the Rule of Law, should you obey the law even when no one is watching?
options: No, only when police are present
Only if you agree with the law
questions.explain: Australians see laws as important for a peaceful and orderly society. Everyone should obey the law at all times or face penalties, and people should keep to the law even when nobody is watching.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Commitment to the Rule of Law

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Do newspapers, television and radio in Australia have freedom of speech?
options: No, the government decides what they publish
Yes, they have the same freedom as people, within the law
questions.explain: In Australia people may speak and write their opinions on any subject, within the law. Newspapers, television and radio enjoy the same freedom, which is an important part of Australia's democracy.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Which of these is illegal in Australia, even though freedom of speech is valued?
options: Writing a letter to a newspaper
Making false allegations or encouraging others to break the law
questions.explain: Freedom of speech in Australia has limits set by law. It is illegal to make false allegations or to encourage others to break the law, and other people's lawful freedom of speech and expression must always be respected.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Is polygamy (having more than one husband or wife at the same time) legal in Australia?
options: No, it is against the law
Yes, if a religion allows it
Yes, if the marriages took place overseas and are kept private
questions.explain: Some religious or cultural practices are illegal in Australia. Polygamy, meaning having more than one husband or wife at the same time, is against the law and can lead to severe penalties, including prison.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: A family wants to arrange their daughter's marriage without her free consent. What does Australian law say?
options: It is allowed if the family's culture accepts it
Forced marriage is against the law and can lead to imprisonment
It is allowed if a religious leader agrees
It is a private family matter
questions.explain: Forced marriage, where one or both people do not freely choose to marry, is illegal in Australia. As with polygamy, it can lead to severe penalties, including prison, whatever the family's cultural or religious views.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Is religious intolerance acceptable in Australian society?
questions.explain: Religious intolerance has no place in Australian society. Everyone should have an equal chance to pursue their own goals and interests, whatever their ethnicity or religion, provided they obey Australian law.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: How does Australian law treat people of different faiths, such as Buddhists and Christians?
options: Only the largest religion is protected
questions.explain: In Australia the law is applied so that nobody receives preferential treatment or suffers discrimination because of their background. For example, Buddhists and followers of every other faith are treated exactly as Christians are.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Equality of all people under the law

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Under Australian law, can two women marry each other?
options: Only if they were married overseas
questions.explain: Australian society values equal rights for everyone, whatever their gender or sexual orientation. Under Australian law, any two people may marry, including two women or two men.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Equality of all people under the law

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: A woman and a man apply for the same job. The woman has better qualifications and skills. Is it her right to get the job ahead of the man?
options: No, men must be chosen first
questions.explain: Discriminating against someone because of their gender is illegal. In Australia, a woman who has better qualifications and skills than a man has the right to be given the job ahead of him.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Equality of all people under the law

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Who has the right to make their own choices about personal matters like religion and marriage?
options: Only the head of the family
questions.explain: In Australia, women and men alike have the right to make their own choices about personal matters such as religion and marriage. The law protects them from intimidation or violence linked to those choices.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Equality of all people under the law

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Can a wife apply to the courts for a divorce even if her husband wishes to continue the marriage?
options: Only with a religious leader's permission
questions.explain: Divorce is accepted in Australia. A wife or a husband can ask the courts for a divorce, even when the other spouse wants the marriage to continue. Both spouses have equal rights.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Equality of all people under the law

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: When an organisation is filling a job, whom does the law support it in choosing?
options: The applicant whose skills and experience best fit the job
A member of the owner's family
The applicant with the most money
Someone of the same ethnicity as the manager
questions.explain: What someone achieves should come from hard work and talent. Jobs should go to people on the basis of skills and experience, not gender, wealth or ethnicity, and the law supports organisations in choosing the person best suited to the role.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Equality of opportunity and a 'fair go'

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: A neighbour has opinions and lifestyle choices very different from your own. What do Australian values expect of you?
options: To listen and respect their views, being tolerant where you disagree
To try to make them change
To complain about them to the police
questions.explain: Australia values mutual respect and tolerance. This means respecting the freedom, dignity, opinions and choices of others, listening to them and respecting their views even when they differ from your own.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Mutual respect and tolerance for others

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Is verbal abuse of another person acceptable in Australia?
options: Yes, if no one is physically hurt
No, violence of any kind, including verbal abuse, is illegal
Only if the person deserves it
questions.explain: Being violent towards another person is against the law. All violence, verbal and physical abuse included, is illegal. Australians believe people can disagree peacefully and have the right to be safe from violence and intimidation.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Mutual respect and tolerance for others

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: What is the age of sexual consent in Australia?
options: 16 or 17, depending on the state or territory
questions.explain: Australia's laws on the age of sexual consent are very strict. The age is 16 or 17, depending on the state or territory. For example, it is illegal everywhere in Australia for a man aged 20 to have sex with a girl aged 15.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Mutual respect and tolerance for others

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: A police officer makes a lawful request of you. What should you do?
options: Ignore it if you are busy
Obey only if the officer is senior
Ask a friend to respond for you
questions.explain: Australians should support the police when they act lawfully. You should comply with any lawful police request, because all Australians commit to obeying the law. The police protect life and property.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Mutual respect and tolerance for others

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Which of these is an example of racism that has no place in Australia?
options: Making racially abusive comments at a sporting event
questions.explain: There is no place for racism in Australia. That includes making or sharing racially offensive material online or in other publications, and making racially abusive remarks in public or at a sporting event.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Mutual respect and tolerance for others

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: What responsibility does everyone in Australia have, when they are able to?
options: To rely entirely on government payments
To try to support themselves and their families
To work only for the government
To leave their family's support to others
questions.explain: Australians expect everyone who lives in Australia to take part in society and contribute to the community. Everyone has a responsibility to try to provide for themselves and their families if they are able to.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: What does the Australian value of 'mateship' mean?
options: Choosing friends from the same background only
Helping each other, especially in times of need
questions.explain: Australians value 'mateship', which means helping one another in hard times. Examples include bringing a meal to an elderly neighbour, giving a friend a lift to see a doctor, or calling in on someone who is lonely, frail or unwell.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Compassion for those in need

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: What must applicants for Australian citizenship whose native language is not English undertake to do?
options: Make reasonable efforts to learn English
questions.explain: English is valued as Australia's national language and something that unites society. People applying for Australian citizenship must commit to making reasonable efforts to learn English if it is not their first language.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: English as the national language

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: You think a neighbour might be planning a serious crime. What should you do?
options: Tell the Australian government authorities without delay
Ignore it as none of your business
questions.explain: Everyone in Australia shares responsibility for helping to protect society. Anyone who suspects that a friend or neighbour may be planning a serious crime should tell the Australian government authorities without delay.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Helping to keep our society safe

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: If a person in Australia sees or knows about a child being abused, what should they do?
options: Report it to the police to investigate
questions.explain: Keeping society safe includes protecting children. Anyone in Australia who sees a child being abused, or knows that it is happening, should tell the police so that it can be investigated.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Helping to keep our society safe

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Which of these is an example of cyber abuse, many forms of which are illegal in Australia?
options: Posting a holiday photo of yourself
Sending a birthday message to a friend
Sharing sexual photos of someone online without their consent
questions.explain: Online abuse, also called cyber abuse, is not accepted in Australia. Examples include posting sexual images or videos of someone online without their consent, stalking someone online, and posting racially abusive comments about a person on the internet.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
ref.section: Part 4: Helping to keep our society safe

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: An Australian citizen is also a citizen of another country. While in Australia, which laws must they follow?
options: Only the laws of their other country
All Australian laws at all times
questions.explain: Australian citizens may hold dual or multiple citizenship where the other countries' laws permit it. However, while in Australia an Australian citizen must obey every Australian law at all times, even if they are a citizen of another country too.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)

questions.chapter: Part 4: Australian values
questions.q: Which of these would undermine Australia's interests and security?
options: Posting official government secrets on social media
Volunteering at a bushfire relief centre
questions.explain: Australian society rests on a shared duty not to harm Australia's interests and security. For example, posting official government secrets on social media would damage Australia's interests and could put other people at risk.

ref.doc: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (CC BY 4.0)
